title: John Bew on British Realpolitik
text:
Podcasts

John Bew on British Realpolitik

November 5, 2026

John Bew joins Jack Dickens to discuss how the British tradition of statecraft grappled with the postwar world. What lessons does it offer today?

Jack Dickens: Hello and welcome to The EI Podcast. This is Jack Dickens, literary editor at Engelsberg Ideas. I’m delighted to be joined today by John Bew, professor of history and foreign policy at King’s College London, biographer of Clement Attlee and adviser to several recent British prime ministers. John, welcome to the podcast. 
John Bew: Thank you very much, Jack. Good to be here. 
Jack Dickens: The UK, like several European countries at the moment, seems to be reaching a crisis point, be it because of the wars raging in Ukraine and the Middle East, the surging energy prices that have emanated from them, or strains in the relationship with the United States. Under Donald Trump, it would be fair to say, Britain has been buffeted by a series of economic and geopolitical shocks. And yet, at the same time, the British government is struggling to find a route towards investing more in defence and security. So my question to you, John, as someone who has advised several recent British prime ministers, and who was advising at the outbreak of the Ukraine war: how serious is the strategic position in which the UK currently finds itself? 
John Bew: Great question, Jack. As we sit here, it’s the morning after the US midterms, and there’s been a so-called blue wave that your listeners will have heard and read about by the time this podcast lands. So Donald Trump has had a big setback in terms of the electoral state of the GOP. We’re also about a week from the fiscal statement by John Healey, in which he committed to finding further money for defence, though that was, of course, deferred, against what others thought might happen at this moment. And as we sit here, there’s a likelihood that the Iran negotiations go nowhere and that there’s a further round of US strikes. 
There’s also growing concern over Ukraine’s ability to finance itself through the winter, its ability to withstand attacks on civilian infrastructure, and Putin’s desire to escalate, certainly in the war in Ukraine over the next few months, and potentially also the fear of a broader escalation in Russia–NATO or Russia–Europe relations. So there are plenty of sources of tumult, concern and tension. This is why you often hear senior former figures from the military and elsewhere talk of a crisis and talk in terms of the threat. I don’t want to underprice any of that. Throw into that the economic situation, which is quite challenging. Throw into that the fact that all the traditional advanced manufacturing democracies, possibly with the exception of the United States, are experiencing stagnation and comparative decline. 
They can’t borrow. They’re vulnerable to debt crises. So it’s not a comfortable position to be in. But, ever the eternal optimist, I’d say that there’s actually plenty the UK can do – as a military power, as a P5 power, as a nuclear power, as the fifth or sixth largest economy depending on how you cut the cake – to help shape the world around it, to protect itself in its neighbourhood and from threats, and to advance the social and economic conditions of the British people. So let’s not despair entirely. There are things you can do in the midst of this, and that requires a certain form of statecraft and some very difficult choices that are hard for politicians to come to. 
So I’m not a doomer when it comes to the state of the UK. There are difficulties and challenges. Maybe just one point on defence, because I think it’s important. The concerns around defence spending, which you brought up, are very important, and they’re often framed as being about the threat, the challenge or the likelihood of war. Yes, that’s really significant. That’s how military planners and the senior top brass should and must think, and that’s what we expect of them. 
But I’d make a bigger case for defence spending, which goes to some of the broader questions. I think we’re at the beginning of a renegotiation of everything in the international order: inputs, outputs, technology controls, export licences, inward investment, tariffs, tech cooperation, defence investment, the relative balance of welfare. Everything is being renegotiated. And what do you want to bring to a renegotiation? You want to bring assets. One asset the UK has traditionally had is serious, professional, effective armed forces. They are currently underfunded. If they are properly funded, that’s a huge asset for Britain diplomatically and economically. So I prefer, A, to be an optimist rather than a doomer, and B, to focus on a positive and assertive case for doing more in defence and security. 
Jack Dickens: So there are causes for optimism. What seems to be missing in a lot of the discussion around the UK’s defence situation is precisely what we need to do in this country to change the mentality surrounding warfare. We’ve seen it recently with comments from the head of the army and the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, about the public having to be prepared for national emergencies, but also for the potential of war. To your mind, what needs to be done to reach the British public with this message and to rewire how our society thinks about the potential of future conflict? 
John Bew: I’ve got maybe bespoke views on this, having seen this issue from inside government and having seen the polling on national security and defence, the good side and the bad side of it, but also as a historian, which gives you some sense of perspective. I think that’s pretty important. First, from inside government. I don’t want to generalise, because it changes, but the polling has told you a couple of things about British attitudes to international affairs. The first is that people in Britain do want the UK to have a role in the world, and do think that role should be as a force for good, or choose your phrase. 
You can see that in the relative levels of support for Ukraine, including when people are asked whether they’re prepared to pay a price at the pump, on energy bills or elsewhere. While that’s tapered off a little over the course of a war that has now lasted longer than the First World War, it’s actually pretty resilient compared with a lot of European countries. So there’s a sense that people want Britain to be strong in the world and engaged in the world, and they understand these security issues – even if some of those hard arguments, like why we should care about a small country in Eastern Europe, to borrow the phrase from the 1930s, are not always easy to make. 
So that fundamental basis is there. Secondly, apart from a small aberration during Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership of the Labour Party, there’s a bipartisan consensus in British foreign policy, and it’s relatively solid. If you look at the debates around defence and security, it’s the opposition telling the government they’re not spending enough. There’s a commitment to the US relationship, no matter who is in the White House. There’s a commitment to NATO. There’s a very real commitment to European security, which is also very important. 
So the foundations are there, in public opinion and in politics, for a serious and consistent approach to the world. I think we’re actually gifted as a nation in that respect. The question the politicians are asking is whether the nation is prepared for war. Well then, what war, and what is required? And here, as a historian, I’d point out that the first opinion polls as we currently understand them were the Mass Observation surveys of 1939 and 1940, which tested the British population’s appetite for war on the eve of and at the start of the Second World War. 
The situation was far worse than it is today. We have a fantasy of wartime cohesion – if only we were as serious as we were then – but British people felt the social contract wasn’t working for them. They’d experienced extremely high unemployment in the inter-war years. They’d experienced the breaking of promises after the sacrifice of the First World War. And things turned around because the social contract was reimagined. Things turned around in the crisis. So the British have a tendency to do all right when the crisis hits. 
Now, does that leave it too late? Often it leaves it pretty close to the wire. And given the nature of modern warfare, what does that look like? But let’s also be frank about what we are actually facing. It’s a different situation from, say, Finland or Estonia, which have a stronger culture of national defence and resilience – literally weapons caches in the forest in the Finnish case, and preparations for total defence in Estonia that encompass everything else. It’s harder for the UK because it’s further away, because we’re an island nation, and because we do things just in time, in a crisis form of government. 
So yes, the messaging is important and I support it. Yes, being more sensible about things like stockpiling is important at this point. But I’m not too despairing of the general state of the British public on this. I’m sticking with my theme of broad optimism about the public getting it when it comes to the threat. The question is what you can change structurally in your political economy to address the threat fully before it comes to your shore. That has been the essence of British defence and security. 
Jack Dickens: When you look at Britain’s position today, what historical parallels come to mind? You’re looking back to the period before the Second World War, but are there other periods in the longue durée of British defence and foreign policy that stand out for you? 
John Bew: Yes. The most obvious is the 1930s. Compared with some of my colleagues and friends, who get impatient with that analogy, I think there are elements in it worth considering, but it’s too easily used as shorthand for “appeasement bad”, unpreparedness and so on. There are questions about the dismantling of the international order and the way that happens systematically, starting with the Japanese invasion of Manchuria and working through Abyssinia and elsewhere, that are pertinent. So we shouldn’t be too swift to dismiss the 1930s analogies, even though, let’s be frank, they are massively overused and have become a kind of acid reflux in British foreign policy debates. 
So let’s look at other periods. There’s the period preceding the First World War. People have talked about it as a period of sleepwalking, of failed diplomacy, of failing to deter or to recognise the nature of the threat before it was too late. I’m particularly interested in the British approach to alliances and diplomacy in this period. There’s a shift from the old tradition of so-called splendid isolation, which is slightly simplistic, to a desire to find alliances and partnerships for Britain that would prevent a war. 
There’s also a general anxiety in Britain from the 1890s through to 1914 about our economic competitiveness, about whether our model works, and in particular about our commitment to free trade, which was the Victorian shibboleth number one. Questions are asked about the relative health of our population and the relative balance of welfare and warfare. It strikes me as quite similar to that period, from late imperial angst through to 1914. In fact, America is going through something very similar. 
The final one I’d mention is the immediate post-war years. People talk in a very excitable and misty-eyed fashion about the creation of the rules-based international order, the liberal international order, and a lot of that story is significant and true, and Britain plays a heroic role. But consider Anglo-American relations from 1945 to 1947, which is supposed to be a golden era. It was hell in Anglo-American relations. The Americans turned off Lend-Lease at a moment’s notice. 
The tap was turned off. Britain was forced to negotiate a massive loan that wasn’t paid off until the end of the last century, and this caused a massive fiscal crisis. The Americans sit on the pound-led economic system and create a dollar-led one. The Americans undercut the British position in the Palestine Mandate – not unjustifiably, in my view, but to catastrophic effect for British interests in the region, causing a massive humiliation and a withdrawal. And the Americans stopped the sharing of nuclear secrets, which had been a wartime commitment, because Congress insisted on it. 
This is also the period in which you build NATO, and the UK takes a real risk in doing so. So it’s important to think of those moments of turbulence, rather than creating a story of a great international order that’s now collapsing. Those international orders are hard fought, hotly contested and fiercely debated. They require risk-taking and derring-do, which was the British position at the start of NATO as well. So we shouldn’t take comforting, soft-sounding lessons from the past, but we can definitely take serious lessons about the hard-headed, unsentimental statecraft that gave us the order we have preserved, and which we see changing today. 
Jack Dickens: I think you’re right that when we think about the challenges facing British leaders today, we can find a number of parallels in the 1950s, whether it’s crisis in the Middle East, the financial entanglements between Washington and London, or the battle to keep Washington engaged with Western Europe’s security, against the backdrop of Russian aggression and the Soviet threat. The key figures in British politics in this period are, of course, the prime minister, Clement Attlee, and his close ally, the foreign secretary, Ernest Bevin. 
Some of our listeners who are not from the United Kingdom might not appreciate the extent to which they were fundamental in keeping the United States engaged with Western Europe, and in finding a patriotic compromise at home that kept the British public invested in the travails of the early Cold War. Could you explain who Attlee and Bevin were, where they came from, and what experiences shaped their approach to British statecraft in this period? 
John Bew: Brilliant. Let’s do the issues first, because they are quite recurrent, to your point, and then we’ll get on to the personalities, because the two are intertwined in significant ways. The issues after the war include, yes, a fear that the Americans will abandon Europe again. Winston Churchill orders the chiefs to run what we’d now call a war game – essentially an assessment of what would happen if the Americans withdrew their troops from Europe. It’s called Operation Unthinkable. The conclusion is that the Soviets would sweep the rest of Europe within days, perhaps weeks. So that lived reality is there. 
And you have, famously, NATO’s first secretary general, Lord Ismay, a Brit, saying the purpose of NATO is to keep the Americans in, the Russians out and the Germans down. Two of those still hold – perhaps not the third. Britain is also in a debate about its approach to Europe and its relative prioritisation of Europe versus the United States, which has echoes today. People forget this all the time: the historical assumption is that a Labour government must have been more pro-European. Not at all. Clement Attlee balks at the idea of deeper European integration, partly because his is the first social democratic majority government in British history, and they want to do things their way. 
They don’t want to be part of a German economic reconstruction plan, and Attlee is fiercely defensive and patriotic about all these issues. So they don’t want to go down the European path. They’re unsure about the United States for a while. They flirt with the idea that Britain can be a third force – a social democratic force standing for the Commonwealth, a third pole in international affairs between Soviet communism on one side and pretty raw American capitalism on the other. In truth, they orient far more towards the American camp, partly because British power is diminishing as the empire is dismantled. 
So those are some of the issues: how to approach European security, how to approach the Russia challenge. And the big test of the international order that comes after the Second World War is, of course, the war in Korea. With a UN Security Council mandate, because the Soviets are boycotting it at that moment, Britain leans in to support the UN-led, US-led mission in Korea, which leads to the Korean settlement we have today. That includes a significant number of British troops dying, and the massive costs of rearmament, which have an effect on the NHS. 
Some of those issues seem quite prescient and relevant; some are obviously distinct. Then, who are the personalities who manage Britain through this period? The one I’ve written about most extensively is Clement Attlee, who comes from what you might call a liberal imperialist, relatively wealthy family. He goes to Haileybury, the empire’s training school, and then on to Oxford. He reads Kipling when he’s young and is deeply patriotic and sentimental – among his early memories is the Diamond Jubilee. He believes in the image of Britain as the greatest nation and greatest empire the world has ever seen, and he is shocked into socialism by what he sees of social conditions in parts of the imperial metropole itself. 
He makes this fateful journey from wealthy, well-heeled Putney in south-west London to the East End, and he is shocked by the condition of people at the centre of the imperial metropolis. 
It shocks him into socialism, but it’s a patriotic socialism. This is a man who goes out of his way to volunteer in the First World War, seeks a commission and becomes Major Attlee; who is the last man off the beach at Gallipoli; who actually believes Churchill’s conception of Gallipoli was sound and the generals botched it; and whose proudest moment is 1940, when he marches into government with Winston Churchill and forms the coalition in which he becomes deputy prime minister from 1942. He regards it as the honour of his life to have worked with Churchill, even though he bests him in 1945. 
This is someone who is deeply patriotic and genuinely internationalist, who doesn’t want to kowtow to Europe or the United States, who believes in a sovereign, strong Britain in the world, and who is deeply sentimental about turning the empire into a Commonwealth. This is Britain’s first socialist prime minister, and he doesn’t fit those stories. Alongside him, as his closest political ally, is Ernest Bevin, who is working on the docks at Bristol from his early teens. He’s an autodidact who teaches himself and rises out of immense poverty – a proper industrial trade union man, who becomes the head of the TUC, the largest trade union in the world, in the 1930s.
So he’s a very consequential political figure outside Westminster, who is only given a seat in 1940, out of the blue. He’s not a political animal; he’s an industrial animal, brought in to mobilise the defence industry and the trade unions for the prosecution of the war. Both of them are hawkish, unsentimental and fearful of the Soviet Union. They’d seen the communists at work in the unions. They were more cold warriors than many American leaders in this period. Deeply patriotic, and fiercely unsentimental and aggressive towards Nazi Germany as well. 
These are the people who form Britain’s post-Churchill government. The personality, the identity, the experience they had – the toughness from wartime and, in Bevin’s case, from mass unemployment and mobilising the unions – make for a very unusual form of British politics. It’s not the current modus operandi, with about a third of our parliamentarians having done the same PPE degree at Oxford and followed the same career path. The average age of Attlee’s cabinet in 1945 was in the early sixties. These were people who had fought and seen friends die in the First World War and who had served in senior government roles in the Second. 
It’s hard to overstate that personal core, as well as the beating heart of British patriotism that was central to everything. 
Jack Dickens: So they’re patriots and realists in international affairs, but fundamentally they are animated by certain ideals – whether it’s Bevin’s project for a Western Union, a political relationship between Western European governments rather than economic and political integration, which he described as a “spiritual union” of the West, or Attlee’s heightened sense of what it means to be a citizen. They are moved by civic ideals that they see as transcending themselves and transcending party politics. I wonder whether that’s something we need to take inspiration from now. Is there a void in our civic life that needs to be reanimated by some of these notions? 
John Bew: It’s a great question. I think those notions do exist, slightly submerged, and the prize goes to the politician who can articulate and harness them. Some come quite close to getting there. Attlee believes in the ethics of Christianity, not the “mumbo jumbo”. He’s not particularly faith-driven or a regular churchgoer, but he holds to the ethics of Christianity and the ethics of citizenship. He reads Gibbon’s Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire at weekends at Chequers. He has a sense of what it is to be an imperial power, and of the responsibilities that come with it. His story of empire is one in which trusteeship really does mean self-government and independence for the imperial dominions. 
He butts heads with Churchill over India in the 1930s. He believes in Indian independence as part of a broader Commonwealth. So there’s absolutely an ethics and a sense of citizenship that come with his patriotism. You mentioned Ernest Bevin articulating what later becomes NATO as a concept. This is a search for what Britain stands for intellectually, ideologically, culturally and politically. There’s a great piece in Engelsberg Ideas, which I’m very happy to refer to, by my good friend and colleague Andrew Ehrhardt, who writes about this episode and Bevin’s commitment to a spiritual union. It’s a really interesting story, because Bevin himself is seen as an unsophisticated bruiser with no formal education. 
A big trade unionist arriving among all these slightly fancy-Dan, aristocratic or well-educated, well-heeled public schoolboys in the Foreign Office, he actually becomes a hero to those diplomats because of his moral clarity and assertiveness. He is, in my view, probably Britain’s second-best foreign secretary ever. He has a clarity that isn’t all diplomatic elision and nuance, and that’s very powerful and changes the course of history. Without it, I don’t think you get NATO as it was constructed. And on the spiritual union specifically, he’s the one who says: this is what we’re standing for. 
What is it? Imagine the post-Second World War period, when you’ve fought two 20th-century wars against different forms of existential threat to what you stand for. So it’s democracy, it’s anti-totalitarianism. But British officials ask: what does he mean by a spiritual union? So they call up an Oxford don called Isaiah Berlin and say: the foreign secretary has said this – what might he mean by a spiritual union? And Berlin defines it very simply: societies that preserve, above all else, individual liberty. That’s the essence of it. In Berlin’s formulation, you can have an individual liberty that requires a more positive, active role for the state – not Berlin’s preferred way, but more Bevin’s. 
Or you can have Berlin’s other formulation, with a negative role for the state – and he means that in an electronic way rather than as a value judgement, as in less state in your life. Bevin is on one side, Berlin on the other, but the fundamental core is individual liberty. So this approach is not just geostrategic; it’s philosophical and values-based. You asked, were they realists? Yes, to a great extent, but with this core of idealism, this vital pursuit of purpose, civilisation and liberty in everything they do. Attlee in some respects becomes even more of an idealist later in life, believing in the United Nations and in a kind of multilateral federation, almost a world state. 
So imagine this period, in which you’ve seen the utter destruction of order, and the thing you have helped give birth to is not a God-given gift inherited by our generation but something you have fought and bled for – blood, sweat and tears. Then think of the ideas that feed into it. It’s very important to see the creation of this order not as a beautiful legal architecture with which well-meaning internationalists and lawyers sat round and eradicated war because they’d found a better way of doing things. It’s so much more than that. 
It’s a receptacle of Enlightenment ideas, of anxieties about the future and about harnessing technology and science. That’s how you’ve got to understand the creation of this order. And it’s ugly. It’s hard fought. It’s quite brutalist at various moments. And yes, it’s realpolitik, but that doesn’t mean it’s not ideological. It’s fundamentally ideological. 
Jack Dickens: As the long-time observer of US foreign affairs Joseph Nye used to say, you should start with realism, but don’t end there. There needs to be some sense of what the realism is for – some purpose animating a country’s behaviour on the world stage. 
I want to turn to some of the uglier aspects you described in the transatlantic relationship in this period, because there were also spectacular fallouts. There’s a fantastic episode you highlight in your biography of Attlee, where Bevin is so offended by the way he’s been spoken to by the US secretary of state, James Byrnes, that he comes back and tells the cabinet, in a roaring, bellowing voice, that we’ve got to have a nuclear weapon and we’ve got to stick a Union Jack all over it. That’s his way of saying that, yes, we need a close relationship with the United States, but we also need our own strategic autonomy. 
Could you speak a bit more about how Attlee and Bevin tried to navigate those storms in the transatlantic relationship in the 1940s? 
John Bew: Yes. It’s not easy. Bevin in particular, because of his trade union connections with the US unions and the Democratic Party, tracks and follows New Deal thinking and ideas. I have three favourite vignettes of wartime and post-war history. The first is when Hitler’s bunker was opened up and ransacked by Soviet troops. They found in it a copy of the Beveridge Report, with comments on it by Nazi officials about what Britain was selling. An abridged version of the Beveridge Report had actually been dropped over Nazi Germany as a statement of our war aims. 
This is what we are fighting for, which is really interesting. The Beveridge Report is the basis of the welfare state, of social insurance and of what becomes the National Health Service. My second favourite vignette comes just before that, during the negotiations over the Atlantic Charter. Churchill is sending telegrams back from Newfoundland, and Attlee makes sure the Labour members of the war cabinet are the quickest to assemble. They comment on the negotiating document and send it back to Churchill, and in doing so they seize on the social welfare provisions that the New Deal Democrats are more willing to put on the line and talk up, including freedom from want and better social insurance, as war aims. 
They elevate those too. So there’s a constant dialogue between these different political instincts. My third favourite vignette is the one you described. To add colour, Bevin had returned from quite a boozy lunch – he’d had a couple of pints of beer, I don’t know precisely how many – and there was a private meeting of the cabinet. And he says, as you say, we’ve got to have one of those things over here, the nuclear bomb, and we’ve got to have a great big bloody Union Jack on it. 
But the first part of that sentence, which is less often quoted, is: I will never again be talked to as a British foreign secretary the way I have been talked to by the US secretary of state, Jimmy Byrnes. It’s a sign of a desire not to be too dependent on the United States. You could argue that ultimately there has been too much dependence on the United States – I’m not making a comment on that either way – but that’s the instinct behind it. I’d say a few more things about the acquisition of nuclear weapons, which happens in a fateful period of British foreign policy. 
January and February 1947. The world turns on a number of issues. The British ask the Truman administration for help in Greece and Turkey to hold the line against communist expansion, because they can’t do it any more, which leads to the Truman Doctrine. It’s when the Marshall Plan is born, which Bevin seizes on – proportionally, the UK receives more Marshall Plan reconstruction money than anyone else. It’s when Attlee announces the end of empire in India. And it’s when the decision is taken to go ahead with the bomb. 
All these things are happening at once, in a two-month period. Everything is in flux, and it’s important to understand just how hot that moment is. The other pressures on the government come from people like John Maynard Keynes and Hugh Dalton, the chancellor of the exchequer, saying Britain faces a financial Dunkirk, that it’s close to bankruptcy, and that industry at home needs the troops back. Britain still has hundreds of thousands of troops overseas, for example in the Suez Canal garrisons in the Middle East. 
We can’t do this any more. We can’t afford to maintain this empire. Attlee’s thinking behind the bomb is actually a recognition that we can’t do defence the way we traditionally did, including in the Indo-Pacific and elsewhere. Remember the fall of Singapore. Our strength and our ability to maintain this empire are curtailed. So the bomb is part of that recognition: we cannot spend so much on conventional defence. 
Jack Dickens: And when Attlee and Bevin try to manage Britain’s retreat from empire, not only in India but also in the Middle East, this again poses problems towards the end of Attlee’s premiership. Bevin, because of ill health and then his death, was no longer foreign secretary by the early 1950s. But what is quite pertinent to what’s going on in the world today is that a crisis emerges in Iran. These are perhaps the earliest moments of a real divergence of interests between the United States and Great Britain over how to manage the Middle East, and in particular the rise of nationalist forces there. 
Could you reflect on that episode, and offer some insight into how it affected the relationship between Europe and the United States in the 1950s? 
John Bew: To zoom out even further: what’s the story of 1815 to 1914? There are lots of stories, but two big parts are the simultaneous decline of two empires, the Austro-Hungarian and the Ottoman. That leads to a crucible of tensions in the Balkans, the eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East, heightened by the Suez Canal, by French and British imperial policies, and by Russian interest in the region. Declining empires fragmenting – partly through internal incoherence, partly because peoples within them seek ethnic, national or other self-determination – are a major disruptive force in the international order. 
Then, in the post-war period, two of the major factors shaping the early Cold War are the sharp decline and dismantling of the British and French empires. That leads to tensions from North Africa to Indochina in the French case, and around the Middle East, India, Pakistan and elsewhere in the British case. And the question America has, of course, is when and how to step in, because as a vacuum emerges, the forces that fill it are often of concern to the United States from a Cold War perspective: Soviet influence, military juntas and so on. 
So that’s the swirl and complexity of post-war politics. You mentioned Bevin becoming increasingly ill and marginalised. What’s very striking is just how unsentimental and how traditionally imperialist his mindset is. At the end of the Second World War, the Soviets, with 20 million dead or however you count it, think: we’ve suffered more than anyone in the Second World War, so what do we get out of it? And one of the things they want – which they still want today – is warm-water ports and access to the eastern Mediterranean. 
They particularly want pieces of modern-day Libya and elsewhere as possessions. How does Ernest Bevin respond? He says the Soviet Union is coming across the throat of the British Empire. So this is not a newfangled internationalism. This is hard imperial realpolitik. Another example you mentioned is Iran, or Persia as it was then understood. Here’s another striking reality. You talked at the start of our conversation about high energy prices. In this period, 40 per cent of the Royal Navy’s oil comes from the Anglo-Persian Oil Company – essentially from British imperial interests in the Gulf, Persia and so on. 
Those dependencies are pretty central to the structure of the British economy. It’s one reason we have a bad energy policy in this period, partly because imperial oil is cheaper oil. So those dependencies become increasingly acute, and they lead to decisions that are understandable – people want cheaper energy amid all these economic pressures – and you can see the flickers of this today. And this is the tragedy of the Middle East: as the European powers move out of it, the things that fill the vacuum require the Americans to become increasingly engaged. 
You see these tensions over the Palestine Mandate, and over what happens with the CIA and the Iranian regime, running right through to 1979 and beyond. These are post-European-empire problems, and they’re pretty acute. Then they acquire a Cold War dimension, which makes them extremely difficult to manage and creates a hell of a lot of bitterness. You see an example of that over Suez, among others. 
Jack Dickens: And this year is the 70th anniversary of the Suez Crisis and the military action by Britain, France and Israel in the Canal Zone in 1956. Is there something in revisiting these episodes to trace the origins of the unequal relationship between the European powers and the United States? One of the things that rankled with the statesmen of the period, in both the Persian oil crisis and the Suez Crisis, was the idea that the United States could make decisions that disproportionately affected Europe economically. 
You mentioned that the Royal Navy was extremely dependent on Persian oil, but Europe’s post-war reconstruction was also dependent on trade and oil flowing through the Suez Canal. And so the United States can make these decisions; it can threaten to crash the pound if Britain and France do not withdraw from Suez. Ultimately, these geopolitical shocks, whether they come from Nasser’s government in Egypt or from nationalist governments in what was then Persia, have a disproportionate effect on Europe’s economic lifelines. 
When we look at that unequal power relationship today – when we see that the war in the Middle East was based on a unilateral decision by President Trump, but one that again has a disproportionate effect on Europe in terms of surging energy prices and the diversion of trade away from the Suez Canal – is there any way to escape this trap, whereby Europe is so geopolitically dependent on the United States and so exposed to decisions taken unilaterally in Washington? 
John Bew: Lesson one from Suez is that people in the Middle East – in this case Arab nationalists under Nasser – have a vote. They have their own ability to effect change and alter the political and geostrategic weather. That lesson has been rerun time and again in different forms, not only Arab nationalist ones. Lesson two for Europe is the bracing one, the tough post-war lesson: acting in a way that is not directly coordinated with the United States, without warning it or negotiating in advance, is a road to ruin and disaster. 
That’s why Suez is such a shock. The two big shocks in British foreign policy in the 20th century, before the 9/11 period, are appeasement and Munich, and Suez. And reflecting on your desire to bring this up to the present, I’d say the following, which goes back to your opening question about the state of the UK. We are uniquely open as an economy. Look at the proportion of US GDP that depends on trade: it’s about 15 per cent. 
That’s minuscule compared with Britain, and it’s partly why the US can get away with a position on tariffs that farmers in Nebraska and elsewhere bristle against, or with a US–Canada trade war that’s hurting Republican candidates in border regions – because trade isn’t fundamental to the core of its GDP. The UK, as a traditional open trading economy, is uniquely exposed to supply-chain disruption, energy disruption and so on, because for many years we’ve depended on offshoring, on just-in-time supply chains, and on the openness and fluidity of the market. 
So when that market is disrupted – two prime examples being Covid and then the Iran war – you’ll notice the UK goes from very high G7 growth projections to collapsing down to sixth or seventh in the G7. You can see this repeated exposure. So what is the nature of the defence policy you need to deal with it? In my view, that steers you towards the importance of the maritime. And I don’t think Europe has fully grasped the importance of the Middle East in the absence of an enlarged US role. 
The story of the last 15 years has been the United States trying to withdraw from an over-commitment. That’s what the US National Security Strategy says, but it’s also what Biden did, what Trump did and what Obama did: a sense that the US was overstretched and too invested in a region when, after all, it is energy independent, even if OPEC matters for its broader energy prices. The extent to which Europe has stepped into that space is underwhelming, to say the least. I sometimes describe British foreign policy in the most recent Middle East wars as one of exquisite irrelevance – in its ability to change the geopolitical weather, to have a say, or to contribute to a coalition mission. 
And you can completely understand why European governments are staying well out of this ill-thought-through Donald Trump adventure. But that’s too comforting politically, because it stops us confronting the strategic reality: unless you have some grasp, some control, some ability to act – even simply when allies and partners in the region, like the Saudis or the UAE, ask you to assert yourself as a security actor – you are simply going to be on the receiving end of the headwinds: disruption, perhaps migration, energy prices, security threats. I think that’s very important, and we’re insufficiently engaged with that reality. 
Jack Dickens: This comes back to the question of what kind of power Britain should be on the global stage, and what principles it should stand for. Traditionally, Britain has been primarily a naval, maritime power – that’s the origin of the British Empire in the 17th and 18th centuries – and it has paid other European militaries to maintain large land armies. Today there seems to be a fixation on potentially stationing British troops in Ukraine as a peacekeeping force, and a focus on landward threats in Eastern Europe. How can we rebalance that discussion and think about a naval or military footprint in the Indo-Pacific and the Middle East? How should that project be pursued? 
John Bew: This is a very difficult question, and it’s one that those involved in military planning, national security strategies and defence strategies have to answer. The truth is that, on current spending, so much goes on the existing equipment programme, and so much is rightly oriented to recapitalising the nuclear programme – and I’d argue AUKUS is additive and supportive of that, but it’s another commitment – that the room to play in other areas is pretty restricted. I must declare an interest as a very proud honorary captain in the Royal Navy. The current First Sea Lord has a concept of a hybrid navy, which would modernise it very significantly and do more in the drone space. But ideally, of course, the First Sea Lord and others would have far more ships. 
There will be more ships built in the next few years on the current trajectory and plan, and simply having more mass – more ships – would of course be a very useful part of that. But again, we’ve run down industrial capacity in this country. Some of our shipyards are ghost towns; some are still running. My own hometown of Belfast is currently building some Royal Navy ships. So that’s one element. But NATO demands things of you as well. NATO demands certain land commitments, and you have to meet those metrics. 
Otherwise you’re called out in a NATO context. But I do agree with the thrust of your question. I support the coalition-of-the-willing proposition. I think the UK is at its best in national security when it is at the sharp end of these contingencies. It can move faster than others. It has more flexible legal and constitutional permissions to be in the vanguard and to bear a significant degree of the risk. You mentioned freedom of navigation: three times under the Conservatives and once under the Labour government, the UK joined the US in operations against the Houthis because of threats to freedom of navigation. 
We were way ahead of the other Europeans on this – not that the Americans noticed or cared, by the way; it’s been quite swiftly forgotten. But that’s the right place for the UK to be. The question is where the plane lands. As things stand, there isn’t really a fundamental choice. There are some capability choices between land and maritime, but the equipment programme and inflationary pressures are so overheated that getting whatever you can on track, in the docks and on the battlefield is the first order of business. If you did have more money on the table, the question would be where and how it is best spent. 
I’m with you – I think, and I’m putting words in your mouth – on a sharper-end, SF-heavy, maritime and air-power-projecting force. That would require you to rethink your relationships with Poland, Germany and others, which have a very strong land focus. That’s something that needs to continue to evolve and be thought through. But I’m saying nothing that anyone in defence doesn’t understand. Ultimately this is a question of public finances. There’s no genius strategic conception sitting outside the building. 
The people in the MoD and elsewhere are managing a difficult proposition, which is an overheated equipment programme. We have to be realistic about that. 
Jack Dickens: Thinking about realpolitik and the coalition of the willing you mentioned, do you foresee any danger from the changing political complexion of Europe itself? We’ve seen Alternative für Deutschland win local elections in Germany, and it seems to be gaining influence over the country’s direction. There’s a very real prospect of Marine Le Pen and her National Rally gaining power in the French presidential election next year. From a British point of view, are you concerned that European rearmament may meet increasing Ukraine scepticism, and a political alignment more sympathetic to Russian aims in Europe? 
John Bew: I guess this is the paradox of the current moment. If you wake up and walk into Number 10 today – or if you’re a member of the Parliamentary Labour Party, where these views are probably held more strongly – you think: I don’t like Donald Trump, I didn’t like Brexit, let’s get more deeply into bed with Europe. The irony and the paradox is that Donald Trump has just taken a massive kicking. There’s a Democratic wave in the United States that fits British Labour or progressive sensibilities far more than Trump does. 
And in Europe you see the worrying emergence of people who do not share your political instincts and views, and who are in fact way beyond even the Conservatives in the UK. It’s striking, by the way, that despite all the turmoil and the many prime ministers of the last few years, Britain again looks like it has a strange degree of stability built into it, partly because of the electoral system and partly because of our political culture. Everyone got overheated. 
But our versions of extremism are comparatively more modulated than those on the Continent. That’s the irony of the present moment, and you can manage through all of it. It’s striking, historically, that the British political clock does not run in perfect synchronicity with the European one, nor with the American one. We’re probably more susceptible to catching a cold from American political fashions and impulses – partly because we’re a monoglot nation – than from European ones. It’s hard. 
It’s hard to think of a progressive or conservative wave that has emanated from Europe and changed the course of British politics. So this is the irony. The Labour Party wants to pursue an ever closer relationship with the European Union while, simultaneously, everyone is batting their eyelids at the five or six runners and riders for the Democratic nomination. So you have odds on a Democrat in the White House in two years’ time. Odds on Marine Le Pen. Probably not odds on the AfD taking the chancellery, but it’s not inconceivable – and probably odds on the AfD increasing its vote share. 
Odds on a little more chaos in Poland. Odds on a significant change of government and quite a lot of disruption in Spain. Odds on Meloni continuing to struggle to balance all these different propositions. Odds on Ukraine looking very difficult over the next few years and draining European energy. Odds on Europe not being able to find and deliver the frozen Russian assets Ukraine might need to stay in the fight. Et cetera. So it’s not a pretty picture. My foreign policy wouldn’t make a false choice between one or the other. 
You need to run a number of horses as hard as you can and think really creatively. I’d put a lot of emphasis on relationships with Germany and with Poland. But I also wouldn’t underplay the importance of the UK–US relationship, even in this period, with two more years of Donald Trump. People sometimes offer this false choice – you’ve got to do one or the other – and I think that’s a real mistake right now. What I would say is that if you were picking a Europe to re-enter, and you’re in the Parliamentary Labour Party or Number 10, you look at it right now and think: crikey, this is not a Europe that can give us particularly good terms. 
More importantly, it’s a Europe that could look extremely different, configuration-wise, in two or three years’ time, and that’s quite hard to manage. There’s no obvious geopolitical alternative to pull off the shelf. Sometimes the debate sounds as if there is. There isn’t. 
Jack Dickens: Do you think the result might be a further strengthening of the UK’s relationship with the Northern European countries – the Scandinavian countries, the Netherlands, but also Poland – and that this might be the bedrock of a Europe that Britain can really be part of, and help to lead? 
John Bew: Yes, to an extent, and I’m a believer in this. When I was involved in government – I can’t overclaim credit – one of the things I pushed and advocated for was an enhanced role for the Joint Expeditionary Force, a Nordic–Baltic alliance, if you like. I deeply believed in that. British people have a soft spot for different forms of Scandinavian politics. There’s a kind of Swedish fetishism, which is good and healthy – cultural, political and otherwise. There’s admiration in the Labour Party for what Mette Frederiksen is doing: quite hawkish and tough on migration, while leading a social democratic party. 
So there’s an obvious community there. There are more shared interests and a greater shared sense of the Russia threat. It’s an obvious community to link up with. And yet, if you look at the better-performing economies in Europe over the last few years: Spain has done pretty well, though it may be hitting the buffers now, and Greece is another. Those are southern European economies with a different view of the security configuration. Poland is the exception in the north in doing pretty well, and Norway is another exception, with its sovereign wealth fund. 
So there’s no easy way of sitting on one side of the map versus the other, and there are limits to that kind of coordination. I’d argue for the most activist, engaged and reflective approach to the northern European states, particularly on defence and technology cooperation. These are all countries, by the way, that keep buying American when it comes to defence tech. I’d play that smart and engage in it very seriously. I think it’s vital. But we’re not going to set up a new Hanseatic League in the next few years. It’s like waiting for the ball to bounce back off the basketball hoop and working out where it’s going to bounce, how you’re going to catch it and what move you’re going to make next. 
The ball is still being thrown. It’s yet to bounce back. 
Jack Dickens: And finally, it would be remiss of me not to ask about what’s just happened in the United States with the midterm elections. We’ve alluded to it many times in this conversation, but some commentators are calling it a blue tsunami, and there are already predictions, as you’ve hinted, that the White House will be occupied by a Democratic president in 2029. How does this change the geopolitical calculus for Britain and Western Europe? Are we likely to see a return to a more Biden-esque engagement with European affairs and geopolitics, or has there been a sea change in America’s strategic posture? 
Will it be increasingly sceptical of European entanglements, regardless of who is in the White House? 
John Bew: It’s hard to generalise. The first job of British diplomacy is to work with the Trump administration for the next two years. That’s very important. It’s the core task and it cannot be under-invested in. You can chase some version of the future, but, for example, if Marco Rubio – which is not inconceivable – were to find his way to the nomination, I suspect Democratic strategists would be very concerned about that presidential race. So I wouldn’t write that off. But clearly there are sharp pendulum swings in US politics. 
That’s how it works. The historian in me says never get carried away by the hyperbole of the moment. But something significant has happened. And you’re right to point out that it’s not going to return to the status quo ante. Biden, generationally and otherwise, had a certain transatlanticism in his DNA that I don’t think naturally exists in the new generation of Democratic national security officials and strategists – who, by the way, are tearing each other’s eyes out. 
There’s a reckoning – fairly or unfairly, and I think a bit unfairly – for anyone who held a senior position in the Biden administration, particularly on the Middle East portfolio, in the sense that they can’t come back. The Democratic Party also has big concerns over its close historic relationship with Israel and its approach to the Middle East more broadly. There’s lots they don’t like about Trump, but there’s going to be no rush back into the arms of Europe or to rebuild an old version of the transatlantic community. What I would say, however, is that if you look at the hard metrics of the transatlantic relationship, they’re really striking. 
They go against everything we might presume from the last couple of years. They go against the idea that Trump is running everything down, and against the idea that the Democrats are never returning to Europe because the future is in the Indo-Pacific. Foreign direct investment and trade in goods and services between Europe as a whole, including the UK, and the United States has never been higher. The share of Europe’s increased defence spending going to US companies has never been higher. Purchasing of advanced US tech and models has never been higher. And Europe has never been more concerned about China, so it looks to the United States on a number of those issues. 
It’s a harder pitch for the United States in the Indo-Pacific. Yes, it’s the future. Yes, the China threat or challenge rightly makes the US more focused on the Indo-Pacific. But look at a country like Australia: is it more economically dependent on trade with the US or with China? China, four times over. The South Korea relationship is not particularly good. Japan – and I love all these countries, travel to them and think we should have very close relationships with them – is struggling with the same debt problems as the UK and France, and is not a massive military spender in that region. 
So against all the odds, and after this period of puerile political nonsense and hostility from parts of the Trump administration – the instinctive preference in some quarters for Putin over Zelensky, the chaos over Greenland and so on – my view, against conventional wisdom, is that if you look at the real, unsentimental, hard metrics, transatlantic relationships remain extremely important. I think that’s worth factoring in. 
Jack Dickens: I think that’s quite an optimistic note on which to end. Thank you very much, John Bew. 
John Bew: Excellent. Thank you so much.
